covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832. Value for sp3; also 73(2)[sp2], 69(1)[sp].

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000a.

polarizability.note: Recommended value of the 2018 table: from experiment where it is precise enough, otherwise from high-level calculation.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('2.00×10² milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('2.8×10¹ milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: solar (photospheric) value; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

temperature.note: The COD entry does not state the temperature of the measurement.

crystal.note: Graphite is the standard state of carbon; diamond is metastable at ambient conditions. Natural crystals, neutron diffraction. Temperature not stated in CIF.

production.basis: mine production, natural graphite (gross weight of graphite)

tonnesPerYear.note: World mine production, natural graphite (gross weight of graphite), 2025 (USGS: 1,800,000 metric tons).

unitValue.note: Price, average unit value of imports, dollars per metric ton at foreign ports: Flake [Graphite (Natural)], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

critical.note: Coking coal is a sedimentary rock/fuel (mostly carbon, with H, O, N, S and ash) used to make metallurgical coke; it is listed as a material, not as elemental carbon. Graphite is a mineral form (allotrope) of carbon; the 2023 study assessed 'natural graphite', the Regulation's critical list says 'graphite'. Strategic entry 'graphite — battery grade' is not restricted to natural graphite: Art. 3(3) asks the Commission to assess at the first review 'whether ... synthetic graphite should remain in the list of strategic raw materials'.

molarHeatCapacity.note: At 25 °C and 1 bar, per mole of atoms, for the form stable at 25 °C (CRC Handbook, 95th ed.).

uses.text: Natural graphite goes into batteries, brake linings, lubricants, furnace linings and steelmaking.
Industrial diamond, about 97 % of it synthetic, cuts and polishes stone, roads and metals, drills for oil and minerals, and is used in making computer chips.
Metallurgical coal is used to make steel.

sectors.text: Essential as of 2026: coal, oil and natural gas, the fossil fuels, are carbon compounds that release energy when burnt, and in 2025 oil and natural gas alone supplied about 38 % and 36 % of the energy used in the United States. Coal is a rock rich in carbon, natural gas is mostly methane (one carbon atom with four hydrogens), and as graphite carbon also goes into batteries.
sectors.page: Coal, Oil and petroleum products, Natural gas; U.S. energy facts explained (2025 shares)

sectors.text: Carbon, mined as natural graphite, goes into vehicle batteries, fuel cells and hydrogen-based steelmaking, according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.
Carbon, mined as natural graphite, goes into the networks that carry data and phones, tablets and laptops, according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.

allotropes.name: Graphite
allotropes.note: Flat sheets of carbon hexagons stacked loosely: soft, black and electrically conducting along the sheets.

allotropes.name: Diamond
allotropes.note: Every atom bonded to four others in a three-dimensional network: the hardest natural material, transparent and insulating.

allotropes.name: Lonsdaleite (hexagonal diamond)
allotropes.note: Diamond's tetrahedral bonding stacked in a hexagonal pattern; found in meteorites and made under shock.

allotropes.name: Fullerenes
allotropes.note: Closed cages of carbon atoms, such as the football-shaped C₆₀, found in 1985.

allotropes.name: Graphene
allotropes.note: A single sheet of graphite, one atom thick, first isolated in 2004.

hazards.note: Aggregated by PubChem from 2727 reports by companies to the ECHA C&L Inventory; the percentage after a statement is the share of reports that give it. 40.2 % of the reports (1095 of 2727) say carbon does not meet the GHS hazard criteria.

crust.note: Earth's crust, as given (mg/kg is parts per million by mass).

ocean.note: Sea water, mg/L read as mg/kg: a litre of sea water is taken as one kilogram (it is slightly heavier; the difference cannot be seen on a logarithmic scale).

body.note: Grams in the 70 kg reference adult of ICRP Publication 23, divided by its mass.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.489, massive_stars 0.511); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 48 px. Cross-check with the paper's text: '49% of C ... produced by AGB stars (at t=9.2 Gyr)' (figure reading 0.489).

bonding.note: Graphite: sheets of carbon hexagons stacked by weak forces. Diamond is a covalent network.

air.text: Bulk graphite or diamond is stable in air at room temperature; fine carbon dust is flammable and freshly made powders can self-heat.

water.text: Insoluble in water and does not react with it.

acids.text: Insoluble in acids and alkalis; only hot oxidising acids attack graphite.

siHistory.text: The mole was the amount of substance containing as many entities as there are atoms in 0.012 kg of carbon-12. Since 2019 it is fixed by the Avogadro constant.

plantRole.text: Taken up as carbon dioxide from the air, or as bicarbonate; a main building block of all organic matter.

humanRole.text: The backbone of proteins, fats, carbohydrates and nucleic acids.

roles.text: The backbone of proteins, fats, sugars and nucleic acids.
The backbone of every organic molecule in a fungal cell.
The backbone of all organic molecules; carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur make up about 97 % of an E. coli cell.
The backbone of all organic molecules; one of the six elements found essential in every prokaryote analysed.

uptake.text: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air; possibly a little bicarbonate from the soil water

known.text: One of the ten elements recognised as essential in the second half of the 19th century, by which time it was known to come from the air

forest.text: The carbon in wood comes from the air. The amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere can itself limit how fast forests grow, a limit that may ease as the gas becomes more plentiful.

isotopeUses.text: Carbon-14, made by cosmic rays in the air, enters every living thing and decays once it dies; in 1949 Arnold and Libby showed that the fraction left dates organic remains, checking it on wood and objects of known age.
Giving algae carbon dioxide labelled with carbon-14 for seconds at a time let Bassham, Benson and Calvin trace the path of carbon in photosynthesis, the cycle now named after them.
Land plants fall into two groups by their ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12; the groups match the two main photosynthetic pathways, C3 and C4, so the ratio tells them apart.

history.note: Known since prehistory as charcoal and soot; Smithson Tennant showed in 1797 that diamond is pure carbon.

prose.text: Carbon is the nonmetal on which all known life is built, and we meet it as soot, pencil graphite and diamond, and in every food, fuel and living cell. Its radioactive isotope carbon-14, made continually by cosmic rays in the upper air, decays with a half-life of 5700 years, which lets archaeologists date wood, bone and seeds up to tens of thousands of years old. A free carbon atom, [He] 2s² 2p², has two unpaired electrons (ground term ³P₀), yet in methane or diamond it forms four equivalent bonds, which chemists describe as one 2s electron being promoted and the orbitals mixing into sp³ hybrids.
